Soirée dialogue : construction identitai: Dialogue Night: Identity Building – Returning to the Homeland
Cinq participantes se sont rencontrées d: Five participants gathered in the La Converse studios to talk about going back to their countries of origin on vacation, and about identity.
Les participantes de la soirée dialogue: The participants in the dialogue night on vacations and going back to the homeland. Photo credit: Emmanuel Leroux-Nega
Pour cette deuxième soirée de discussion: For this second evening of discussion on identity building, we wanted to explore a specific theme: how does going back to your country of origin, or not, influence the way Montréal youth build their identity?
Cinq participantes se sont retrouvées da: Five participants gathered in our studios. Coming from different backgrounds and continents, each one shared a unique experience, shaped by her relationship to her country of origin and by her own personal journey.
Dans le cadre de ce reportage, j’ai coll: For this report, I worked with Jade Assayag on research and with Emmanuel Leroux-Nega on camera. Both took part in the evening to make sure the dialogue ran smoothly. Emmanuel and I also tested a new equipment setup to improve sound and image quality. Looking back, I think this somewhat imposing setup may have intimidated our participants, who took a while to feel at ease and to talk more freely.
Mais une fois la glace brisée, la discus: But once the ice was broken, the discussion proved rich, sincere and full of shared experiences.
Le studio de La Converse est baigné d’un: The La Converse studio is bathed in dim light. The chairs arranged around the wooden table are reminiscent of an evening friends might spend talking in a dining room. Conversations start off softly, and laughter bursts out here and there. The participants arrive little by little, greet each other shyly and take their seats. For this edition of our dialogue night, a few curious onlookers are on hand as an audience.
Il est 18 h 30 quand tout le monde prend: It’s 6:30 p.m. when everyone settles in. The microphones are set up podcast-style, which allows each person to share her experiences in a natural conversation.
<strong>Retourner au pays : entre retrou: Returning to the homeland: between reunion and distance
Julie est la première à se lancer. Elle: Julie is the first to jump in. She was born in Montréal to Vietnamese parents. She speaks with confidence and firmness, but her tone softens when she talks about Vietnam. “Before, I used to say I was going on a trip. Now I say I’m going home to see family,” she says with a smile. Her trips back have become an anchor: “The more I go, the stronger my ties get.”
À ses côtés, Ioana se redresse. Elle est: Beside her, Ioana sits up straight. She arrived from Romania at the age of four. Her first trip back, eight years after she arrived, left a mark on her: “All that time, I had built an idea of the country through my parents’ stories. By finally going there, I was able to form my own opinion.” But she also noticed a gap. “For my parents, Romanian identity is tied to communism. For the people there today, it’s not that anymore,” she explains.
Tian enchaîne. Elle est née en Chine. «: Tian follows. She was born in China. “When I was little, I was always asking my parents, ‘When are we going back?’” she says with a little laugh. But over the years, her relationship to China has changed. “Now I feel like a visitor there. Canada has become my home,” the young woman says.
Imen prend ensuite la parole : « Je ne s: Imen speaks next: “I’ve only been back to Algeria once since I immigrated,” she says. Her voice trembles slightly. “Seeing my family again brought me comfort, but also a lot of sadness. You realize what you’ve lost. Faces change, kids grow up… and so do we.” Julie, moved by her story, nods. She adds softly: “Sometimes I wonder, if my parents are no longer around, what my connection to Vietnam will be.”
<strong>Être de « là-bas » sans y avoir: Being from “over there” without having grown up there
Solemani, qui est née en Belgique et est: Solemani, who was born in Belgium and is of Congolese origin, takes over. She has never set foot in the Congo, even though she has tried to go several times. “I’m very chauvinistic when it comes to my country: for me, the Congo is the best country in the world!” She laughs, but her tone then becomes more serious. “Here, when I meet Congolese people who grew up there, I’m often reminded that I’m not a ‘real’ one,” she says. Today, she tries to get closer to her roots through her sociology studies. Her research topics are often tied to Congolese culture.
Peu à peu, la conversation glisse vers l: Little by little, the conversation drifts toward language. Imen explains that she has “a different personality depending on the language” she speaks. Julie sometimes surprises herself by understanding the mistakes she makes in French: “I realize it comes from Vietnamese. Language structures the way we see the world.”
<strong>Et si l’on ne pouvait plus y ret: And what if we could no longer go back?
Puis une question surgit : que deviendra: Then a question arises: what would become of that connection if a pandemic kept them from returning to their country of origin for 20 years?
Imen croit que l’identité résisterait gr: Imen believes identity would hold on thanks to social media, music, food, and the cultural elements she would stay in contact with. Solemani adds a nuance: “Even without internet, the Congo runs in my veins. Even if it’s true that you miss the updates, the culture keeps evolving without us.” Ioana adopts a calmer tone: “In the short term, identity holds. But over several generations, it changes. It becomes a blend, a new culture.”
Dans le cercle, chacun semble réfléchir: In the circle, everyone seems to be reflecting on what it means to grow up with a plurality of identities. Solemani sums up what they all express: “We’re neither one nor the other, we’re a mix of both.”
Des sourires apparaissent, les hochement: Smiles appear, and the nodding multiplies. The evening ends on a warm note. After an hour and a half, the discussions fade gently, making way for a question period started by members of the small audience. Summer is made for play, but for some, vacations awaken reflections on identity. The conversations continue quietly as the microphones and cameras are switched off. The participants and the audience seem to still have things to say to each other.
